sources.title: Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June
sources.summary: Unit 42 investigates network compromises across numerous industries
sources.text: cyber-crime Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June Unit 42 investigates network compromises across numerous industries Jessica Lyons Jessica Lyons Cybersecurity Editor Published tue 20 Oct 2026 // 18:33 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk 2 hours ago LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets 7 hours ago Signal bug could keep your mic - and camera - on after hangup 9 hours ago PHP devs publish critical bug fix as site owners warned: Pull 'em offline if you're unpatched 10 hours ago AI has 'potential' to turn script kiddies into sophisticated infrastructure attackers 14 hours ago Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing. CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection. The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation. REG AD That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17. REG AD On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE. “Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42. After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned. In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail." Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected. Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators , are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions. “The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).” This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added. REG AD Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27532 , which targets Veeam backup infrastructure. So if you haven’t already patched vulnerable PAN-OS software, do so now - and investigate whether attackers have already gained access to your network. Check Unit 42’s indicators of compromise to assist with threat-hunting activities.® palo alto networks cyber-crime pan-os ransomware security Make us preferred on Google

sources.title: 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water
sources.summary: ICO reprimands Ogi Networks and Data Cymru after ransomware breach exposes info of 3,300 people, mostly children
sources.text: cyber-crime 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water ICO reprimands Ogi Networks and Data Cymru after ransomware breach exposes info of 3,300 people, mostly children Paul Kunert Paul Kunert EMEA EDITOR Published tue 20 Oct 2026 // 14:35 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk 2 hours ago LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets 7 hours ago Signal bug could keep your mic - and camera - on after hangup 8 hours ago PHP devs publish critical bug fix as site owners warned: Pull 'em offline if you're unpatched 10 hours ago AI has 'potential' to turn script kiddies into sophisticated infrastructure attackers 14 hours ago A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru. According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data. REG AD On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server. REG AD "Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF]. ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru. "ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'." The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second. "The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added. "ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years." The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory. The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements. REG AD "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. "The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ® united kingdom ico password security cyber-crime Make us preferred on Google

sources.title: Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’
sources.summary: Massive clean-up job under way because this mess makes it possible to impersonate any website or service
sources.text: security Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’ Massive clean-up job under way because this mess makes it possible to impersonate any website or service Simon Sharwood Simon Sharwood APAC Editor Published tue 20 Oct 2026 // 23:57 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE 'People's Panel' to check if UK wants controversial Digital ID will cost £630K April 1, 2026 New SSL/TLS certs to each live no longer than 47 days by 2029 April 14, 2025 Google says it's rolling out fix for stricken Chromecasts March 13, 2025 As Chromecast outage drags on, fix could be days to weeks away March 13, 2025 Get off that old Firefox by Friday or you'll be sorry, says Moz March 13, 2025 Tragically simple private keys used by a certification authority based in India have been compromised, meaning the 60-million-plus certs it has issued can’t be trusted and necessitating a massive clean-up job. The CA of concern in this case is called eMudhra, which boasts of having issued over 60 million digital certificates to help usher in a world of digital trust. The company has instead panicked the world. REG AD News of the company’s errors appeared on Tuesday in a post by Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s cryptography engineering team. REG AD “On Saturday, October 17, at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report from a community member that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had been compromised,” he wrote . “These keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control.” Or as Cloudflare put it , “an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.” Jackson has since elaborated on the incident and the response, which has thankfully seen Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple remediate the issue so their browsers won’t rely on the certificates – at least after users install an update. He also reports that eMudhra has revoked the certs, and lists many FOSS projects that have issued updates that mean they won’t recognize certs from eMudhra. That’s welcome, but sadly certs signed with these private keys are still out there and many services rely on them. Browser makers are set up to detect and reject bad certs. Others who relied on them may not be, and will likely need to dig into their environments to see if they rely on certs signed by eMudhra. Developer Geoffrey Huntley has offered some advice on automating that process. At the time of writing, eMudhra has not responded to The Register ’s inquiries about the incident and its security practices. The latter question is of great interest because security researcher Scott Helme analyzed eMudhra’s certs and found one the private keys it used “is the number 4.” “Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4... Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second,” Helme wrote. Other researchers have found private keys including the numbers 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237. REG AD Those are vastly inadequate keys, because they’re easy to guess, making all certs issued by eMudhra susceptible to brute force attacks. As Helme put it: “A P-384 private key should be a random 384-bit number, which gives you 2³⁸⁴ possibilities (or roughly 10¹¹⁵), so nobody is ever going to search that.” This is a developing story and The Register will update it as more information becomes available. ® digital certificate security Make us preferred on Google
